cards.name: Noise reduction that keeps detail
cards.summary: Cleans luminance grain and coloured blotches from a high-ISO or phone photo while keeping edges, then restores a touch of crispness.
use_for: low-light event and concert photos
phone photos and video frame grabs
photos that will be enlarged or printed
before a heavy grade that would amplify noise
avoid: pushing it until skin and walls look waxy: stop when the noise is just less visible
RAW files: denoise in Camera Raw or with AI Denoise first (both have no script route here), they beat any filter on a rendered photo
CorelDRAW Remove Noise: weak in the render test (barely visible change); this recipe uses Median and Smart Blur there instead
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object, so the filters that follow are editable smart filters with their own mask.

Filter > Noise > Reduce Noise for the coloured blotches (Reduce Color Noise 45 %). Untested: the noise-free test plate gave it nothing to clean (verdict not_rendered), so this step caps the recipe at medium; Strength / Preserve Details travel in the channelDenoise object, which a plan cannot carry.

Filter > Blur > Surface Blur, small: averages only similar neighbours, so grain melts while edges stay (the render at 40 / 40 airbrushed flat areas; 3 / 10 is a light clean-up). Mask it off fine texture you want to keep.
Filter > Sharpen > Smart Sharpen, gentle (Amount 60, Radius 0.8, Lens Blur) to restore the edge crispness lost to the clean-up.
Effects > Noise > Median at its smallest radius: specks vanish, edges stay fairly crisp (large radii turn the image to blobs, as the render showed).
Effects > Blur > Smart Blur (dialog label Amount, key Detail): smooths low-contrast grain, keeps strong edges (render at 100 airbrushed the wood).
Effects > Sharpen > Unsharp Mask, gentle, so edges read crisp again.

manual_steps: For the best result on RAW or heavy noise: Filter > AI Denoise or Filter > Camera Raw Filter > Denoise by hand (no script route harvested).

cards.name: Output sharpening for print
cards.summary: Final sharpening at the exact print size and resolution, stronger than looks right on screen because ink spread and paper soften the image.
use_for: photos in brochures, posters and magazines
large-format prints and banners
photo books and certificates
avoid: sharpening before resizing: always size to the final print dimensions first
halos on high-contrast edges: lower Radius before Amount
sharpening noise: denoise first
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Image > Image Size: resample to the final print size at 300 ppi (or the printer's figure); verified live with bicubic.
Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object, so the filters that follow are editable smart filters with their own mask.

Filter > Sharpen > Smart Sharpen: Amount 180, Radius 1.5 px at 300 ppi (about 1 px per 200 ppi), Remove Lens Blur, More Accurate on. On screen at 100 % it should look slightly crunchy; the render at 300 / 4 showed what over-sharpened halos look like.
Effects > Sharpen > Unsharp Mask on the placed bitmap at its final size: Percentage 150, Radius 2, Threshold 3 spares smooth areas (the render at 300 / 8 / 0 gave wide halos).

manual_steps: Check at 100 % (Photoshop View > 100 %) and in a test print if the job matters; output sharpening is judged on paper, not on screen.

cards.name: Output sharpening for screen and social
cards.summary: Downsize to the exact pixel size the platform shows, then sharpen lightly so the photo stays crisp after scaling and compression.
use_for: Instagram, LinkedIn and YouTube images
website hero images and thumbnails
email and newsletter photos
avoid: sharpening at full camera resolution and letting the platform downscale: the sharpening disappears and artefacts remain
strong sharpening before heavy JPEG compression: halos turn into ringing
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Image > Image Size: resample to the output pixel size (e.g. 1080 px wide for a feed post).
Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object, so the filters that follow are editable smart filters with their own mask.
Filter > Sharpen > Smart Sharpen at screen size: Amount 80, Radius 0.5 px, Remove Lens Blur.
Effects > Sharpen > Unsharp Mask after the bitmap is at its output size: Percentage 70, Radius 1.

manual_steps: CorelDRAW: resample the bitmap to the output size first with Bitmaps > Resample (the menu only opens the dialog; ActiveShape.Bitmap.Resample is the unverified object-model route), or export at the target size.

cards.name: High Pass detail sharpening
cards.summary: A non-destructive sharpening layer: the photo's fine detail isolated with High Pass and blended back in Overlay or Soft Light, adjustable by layer opacity and mask.
use_for: sharpening only the eyes, product edges or type in a photo (mask the rest)
adding crispness to architecture and products
an editable sharpening layer that can be toned down later
avoid: large radii: they add a halo glow instead of crispness; 1-4 px is sharpening, more is local contrast
noisy photos: High Pass sharpens the noise as well
CorelDRAW: its High Pass works (render pass) but PGD has no scripted overlay merge for a bitmap copy; use Unsharp Mask there
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Duplicate Layer: work on a copy above the original.
Image > Adjustments > Desaturate on the copy (a pixel layer, so before any smart object conversion): removes the colour fringes High Pass leaves.
Filter > Other > High Pass, Radius 3: the copy turns flat 50 % grey with only the edges left (as the render showed at 15).
Set the copy to Overlay (Soft Light for a gentler result): grey disappears, edges get contrast. Opacity 50-100 % sets the strength; a layer mask limits it to where you want it.

cards.name: Remove objects and blemishes
cards.summary: Unwanted objects, signs, wires, spots and blemishes disappear into their background: selected, then filled with texture synthesised from the surroundings.
use_for: removing distractions from product, travel and real-estate photos
cleaning backgrounds before a cut-out or a text overlay
removing dust, small blemishes and stray hairs in portraits
clearing space for type in a hero image
avoid: news and documentary photos: removing or adding content misrepresents the event
objects that overlap complex structure (fingers, faces, text): fills invent wrong detail; use the Clone Stamp by hand
Generative Fill and Generative Upscale spend credits and have no script route here
CorelDRAW: it has no healing, clone or content-aware tools (Corel PHOTO-PAINT does); do this in Photoshop.
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: With the object selected (by hand, see manual steps), Select > Modify > Expand by 6-10 px so the fill samples clean background beyond the object's edge.

Edit > Content-Aware Fill (executeAction 'cafWorkspace'): verified live, with no settings it applied the workspace defaults and put the fill on a new layer, so the original stays untouched. Needs an active selection.
Select > Deselect.

manual_steps: Select the object by hand: Lasso, or the Object Selection Tool (its detection inside a drawn rectangle has no script route); Select > Subject only helps when the object is the main subject.
Small spots and blemishes: Spot Healing Brush Tool or Remove Tool on a new empty layer with Sample All Layers on (neither brush can be scripted).
Edges that the fill gets wrong: Clone Stamp Tool by hand on the same cleanup layer.
Large removals where invented content is acceptable: Edit > Generative Fill with an empty prompt (credits, no script).

cards.name: Scan clean-up: dust, scratches and moire
cards.summary: Removes dust specks, fine scratches and the wavy moire of scanned printed pictures, then restores a little crispness.
use_for: scanned old photographs and archive prints
scans of printed brochures or newspaper pictures (halftone moire)
dusty film scans
avoid: global Dust & Scratches at a large radius or zero threshold: the whole image turns blotchy (as both apps' renders showed); keep the radius small and mask it to the damaged areas
fine detail such as type or hair: it vanishes with the dust; mask it out
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object, so the filters that follow are editable smart filters with their own mask.
Filter > Noise > Dust & Scratches, Radius 2 / Threshold 15: removes specks that differ from their neighbours; paint the smart-filter mask black where real detail suffers.
Filter > Noise > Median, Radius 2, only for halftone moire from printed originals (skip it for photo scans): smooths the screen pattern.
Filter > Sharpen > Smart Sharpen, gentle, to bring back edges after the clean-up.
Effects > Correction > Dust and Scratch: Radius 2, Threshold 40 (the render at 10 / 8 smeared everything; a higher threshold spares real detail).
Effects > Noise > Remove Moire for scans of printed pictures (the plate had no halftone, so only its slight softening was rendered).
Effects > Sharpen > Unsharp Mask, gentle.

manual_steps: Large scratches and tears: Spot Healing Brush or Clone Stamp by hand in Photoshop.

cards.name: Dodge and burn on a grey layer
cards.summary: Non-destructive local lightening and darkening on a 50 % grey Soft Light layer, to sculpt light, add depth and guide the eye.
use_for: portrait and product sculpting
evening out uneven light across a photo
adding depth and a vignette-like focus by hand
retouching that must stay editable
avoid: dodging and burning on the photo pixels themselves: destructive and hard to undo
strong strokes: build up with many low-exposure (5-10 %) passes
CorelDRAW: it has no healing, clone or content-aware tools (Corel PHOTO-PAINT does); do this in Photoshop.
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > New > Layer above the photo.
Edit > Fill with Contents 50 % Gray (the fill descriptor's Usng = 50 % grey instead of the foreground colour), 100 % opacity, Normal.
Set the grey layer to Soft Light: 50 % grey is neutral, so nothing changes until you paint (the card lists exactly this use; its frame matched the Soft Light formula).

manual_steps: Paint on the grey layer with the Dodge Tool / Burn Tool (Range Midtones, Exposure 5-10 %) or with a soft Brush in white (lighten) and black (darken) at 5-10 % opacity. Scripts can only replay strokes along a path (PathItem.strokePath), so the painting is by hand.

cards.name: Skin smoothing that keeps texture
cards.summary: Evens out skin tone and small irregularities with an edge-preserving blur on a masked copy, then adds back fine grain so pores and texture still read.
use_for: beauty and headshot retouching
corporate profile photos
close-up portraits for print and social
avoid: smoothing the whole photo: eyes, brows, lips and hair must stay sharp; mask to skin only
high opacity: plastic, airbrushed skin; 40-70 % is usually enough
changing someone's appearance beyond clean-up in news or documentary photos
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Duplicate Layer: work on a copy above the original.
Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object, so the filters that follow are editable smart filters with their own mask.
Filter > Blur > Surface Blur on the copy: flat areas melt, strong edges stay (the card warns that pushed hard it gives plastic skin).
Filter > Noise > Add Noise as a second smart filter: Gaussian, monochromatic, 1-2 %, so the smoothed areas get back a fine texture.
On a duplicate of the bitmap: Effects > Blur > Smart Blur, edge-preserving smoothing.
Uniform Transparency 40 on the smoothed copy (about 60 % opacity) so the original texture shows through.

manual_steps: Photoshop: lower the copy's layer opacity to 40-70 %, add a black layer mask (Alt-click Add Layer Mask) and paint white over the skin areas only.
CorelDRAW: draw a shape around the skin areas by hand and PowerClip the smoothed copy into it (Object > PowerClip), so eyes and hair come from the sharp original.

cards.name: Straighten and fix converging verticals
cards.summary: Levels a tilted horizon and makes leaning building edges vertical again, then crops or fills the empty wedges.
use_for: architecture and real-estate photos
product shots taken at an angle
scans that went in crooked
event photos with a tilted horizon
avoid: strong corrections on a tight crop: the stretched edges lose resolution; shoot wider
perspective fixes on faces near the frame edge: they distort
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object, so the filters that follow are editable smart filters with their own mask.

Filter > Lens Correction: Rotation Angle levels the horizon (sign as in the dialog; rotation was not separated in the render), Vertical Perspective pulls converging verticals upright (the render at -20 keystoned the frame clearly); tune both per photo.
Bitmaps > Straighten Image: InvokeItem only opens the dialog; align the straightening bar, correct perspective and crop to the result there (no object-model equivalent).

manual_steps: Photoshop: crop the empty wedges with the Crop Tool (Document.crop(bounds, angle) by script), or select them and run Edit > Content-Aware Fill.
Several planes (a building corner): Edit > Perspective Warp by hand (interactive only).

cards.name: Upscale for print or large display
cards.summary: Enlarges a small photo to print or banner size with detail-preserving resampling, then cleans and sharpens the result.
use_for: web-resolution images that must go to print
old small photos for a poster or banner
crops that need more pixels
avoid: expecting real detail from a tiny source: 2x is safe, beyond 3-4x faces and type look invented or mushy
upscaling a noisy or JPEG-damaged image: clean it first (denoise / JPEG artefact recipes)
AI and generative upscalers invent detail: not for news or evidence photos
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Image > Image Size: Resample on, enlarge to the target (e.g. 200 %); choose Preserve Details 2.0 in the dialog (the scripted route verified in the harvest used bicubic).
Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object, so the filters that follow are editable smart filters with their own mask.
Filter > Blur > Surface Blur, very light: evens out the resampling noise.
Filter > Sharpen > Smart Sharpen at the new size, Amount 120, Radius 1.2.
Bitmaps > Resample: the dialog's machine-learning upsampling modes rebuild detail when enlarging. InvokeItem only opens the dialog; ActiveShape.Bitmap.Resample is the unverified object-model route.
Effects > Sharpen > Unsharp Mask after the enlargement.

manual_steps: Bigger jumps: Image > Generative Upscale (credits, no script route) or Camera Raw's Super Resolution (2x, by hand).

cards.name: Dehaze a washed-out photo
cards.summary: Cuts haze, smog or a foggy window look: deeper contrast and colour in the washed-out areas, a little midtone clarity.
use_for: landscape and city photos shot through haze or smog
photos taken through glass
flat, low-contrast drone shots
faded scans
avoid: strong Dehaze on skies: banding and dark corners; keep it under 50 and mask the sky if needed
photos that are meant to look atmospheric
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Clarity and dehaze adjustment layer: Dehaze 35 cuts the haze, Clarity 10 adds midtone bite (the render at 60 / 50 was strongly darker, crisper and more saturated).
Brightness/Contrast layer: Brightness +4 if Dehaze made the photo too dark.
Color and vibrance layer: Vibrance +10 for colour that the haze had washed out.
Effects > Adjust > Auto Adjust: stretches each channel to full range, the main dehaze move on a foggy photo.
Effects > Adjust > Gamma 0.9: slightly deeper midtones.
Effects > Adjust > Vibrance +20 for the washed-out colours.

cards.note: Photoshop plan is render-verified (Clarity and dehaze pass); the CorelDRAW plan has no dedicated dehaze and approximates it with a channel stretch.

cards.name: Fix lens faults: colour fringes, vignetting, distortion
cards.summary: Removes the camera lens's colour fringes along high-contrast edges, brightens dark corners and straightens barrel distortion with manual Lens Correction sliders.
use_for: wide-angle architecture and interior photos
product shots on white with fringed edges
cheap-lens and phone photos with dark corners
avoid: photos with lens metadata: the automatic profile corrections in Camera Raw are better and need no slider guessing
creative vignettes you want to keep
CorelDRAW: lens distortion lives in Bitmaps > Straighten Image (dialog only, see the straighten recipe)
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object, so the filters that follow are editable smart filters with their own mask.

Filter > Lens Correction, Custom sliders: Distort Amount pulls barrel distortion straight, Aberration Red-Cyan / Blue-Yellow shift the colour channels to remove fringes, a positive Vignette Amount brightens dark corners. Only the vignette (negative) and the perspective sliders were separated in the render, so tune these on screen.

manual_steps: Zoom to 200 % on a high-contrast edge in a corner to judge the fringe sliders.
RAW or JPEG with lens metadata: Filter > Camera Raw Filter > Optics (Remove Chromatic Aberration, Use Profile Corrections) by hand.

cards.name: Clean JPEG compression artefacts
cards.summary: Softens the blocky 8x8 tiles, edge ringing and smeared colour of an over-compressed JPEG before it is reused, enlarged or printed.
use_for: images saved from chat apps and social platforms
low-quality stock or client-supplied JPEGs
web images that must go to print
avoid: re-saving as JPEG at low quality afterwards: the artefacts come straight back; save PNG or high-quality JPEG
expecting lost detail to return: it smooths damage, it does not rebuild texture
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object, so the filters that follow are editable smart filters with their own mask.

Filter > Noise > Reduce Noise with Remove JPEG Artifact on and Reduce Color Noise 30 % for the colour smear. Untested: the plate has no JPEG blocks (verdict not_rendered), so this caps the recipe at medium; the render did show Reduce Color Noise 100 % bleeding colour across hard borders, so keep it moderate.
Filter > Blur > Surface Blur, light: flattens the remaining block edges in smooth areas while real edges stay.
Bitmaps > Remove JPEG Artifacts: CorelDRAW's machine-learning clean-up, applied straight from the menu with no dialog (InvokeItem). No render test exists for menu commands.
